frameworks.name: What-Who-When Copy Framework
frameworks.definition: A multi-angle copywriting structure derived from the value equation: address dream outcomes (speed, likelihood, ease) and nightmare scenarios (pain, fear) to produce varied ad copy that reaches the broadest set of qualified avatars.

frameworks.name: Front-End / Back-End Offer Ladder
frameworks.definition: A two-stage offer architecture where a low-friction front-end product (~$5k) closes fast on one call, converts prospects to customers, and funds the cash outlay while seeding the upsell into the core high-ticket back-end product ($30k+).

frameworks.name: Milestone Upsell Sequence
frameworks.definition: Three timed upsell attempts during a short engagement window: (1) at the first measurable win, (2) one week later, (3) last-chance before the window closes; each attempt is easier because the client is now a paying customer experiencing results.

frameworks.name: Waive-Fee Close
frameworks.definition: An offer structure in which the seller waives the upfront implementation fee in exchange for a multi-quarter commitment; the buyer chooses between paying the fee and staying month-to-month or committing long-term and getting the fee waived.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a back-end upsell conversion rate below 20% is a reliable signal of an offer problem on either the front end, back end, or both. A healthy offer ladder should convert well above that threshold once the avatar fit is correct.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Back-end upsell presented after core offer purchase
claims.mechanism: Below-20% upsell conversion indicates the front-end product either attracts the wrong avatars or fails to create enough perceived necessity for the back-end, so most buyers exit rather than ascend.

numbers.axis: back-end upsell conversion rate (as signal of offer health)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for a small restaurant or bar business owner, an appropriate customer acquisition cost (CAC) is roughly $1,500 to $3,500; Unfiltered Hospitality's CAC of ~$12,000 is three to eight times the appropriate range, indicating a severe offer mismatch or broken sales process.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B service targeting small restaurant/bar owners
claims.mechanism: An outsized CAC relative to the front-end price signals that either the offer is attracting misaligned traffic or the sales process is too friction-heavy, forcing multiple calls and long cycles that drive up cost per close.

numbers.axis: customer acquisition cost (CAC) appropriateness by business segment

anchors.region: acceptable range for small restaurant B2B service

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that selling a $30,000 high-touch service offer to cold-traffic prospects via a single call funnel is the wrong sequencing. The right offer at the wrong time is still the wrong offer; a high-ticket product requires either a much longer trust-building sales process or a lower-barrier entry offer that converts the prospect into a paying customer first.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Cold prospects lack the trust and information required to commit $30,000 in a single interaction; the multi-call close that results compounds cost per sale and creates high drop-off at each step.
bounded_by: If advertising is primarily brand-based and inbound, prospects arrive with enough prior information to justify going straight to the high-ticket offer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends a front-end offer priced at $5,000–$6,000 that solves one specific, immediately measurable problem. This enables a one-call close, converts prospects to customers, and generates cash to offset advertising spend before the back-end upsell is attempted.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Existing customers are approximately 10x more likely to buy again than cold prospects; lowering the bar to the first transaction shifts the relationship from prospect to customer and dramatically raises back-end close probability.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that the call-out line in an ad—identifying the specific avatar in one phrase (e.g., '$4 million-plus per year restaurant owners')—accounts for approximately 80% of the work of advertising, because it self-selects the right audience before any further persuasion is needed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Precise avatar call-outs filter unqualified readers immediately and make qualified readers feel the ad is specifically for them, dramatically increasing relevance and click-through before the hook or body copy do any work.

numbers.axis: share of advertising effectiveness attributable to avatar call-out

anchors.region: hook, body copy, and creative contribution (combined remainder)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the ability to articulate a prospect's pain more precisely than they can articulate it themselves is a stronger trust signal than any positive promise, because the prospect infers that the seller fully understands their problem and therefore can solve it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cold or warm prospect who has not yet experienced a result from the seller
claims.mechanism: Precise pain articulation demonstrates specific contextual knowledge; contextual knowledge is a credible proxy for solution capability; this proxy is more persuasive than aspirational claims which prospects cannot yet evaluate.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that a good lead-magnet landing page should convert at approximately 30%; Unfiltered Hospitality's landing page was converting at approximately 7%, indicating roughly a 4x improvement opportunity solely from landing page optimization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Direct response landing page for a lead magnet offer

anchors.region: Hormozi benchmark for lead-magnet landing page

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that friction in a sales funnel has an optimal level: too little friction (e.g., just a phone number and price) brings unqualified buyers; too much friction (e.g., repeated opt-in fields, slow load times) eliminates both good and bad prospects. The appropriate friction level scales with price: higher-priced products require and can sustain more friction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Friction calibration depends on offer price point
claims.mechanism: Qualification friction filters unqualified prospects (good friction); process friction such as repeated forms or slow loads drives away both qualified and unqualified buyers without any filtering benefit (bad friction).
bounded_by: Does not apply to high-brand-equity inbound funnels where prospects are pre-sold before reaching the funnel.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that a pre-call video (VSL) be delivered and confirmed watched before the sales call begins. The VSL replaces the repetitive early-call pitch, which becomes stale and disengaged when delivered verbatim dozens of times; the call then begins at the decision stage rather than the information stage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B service sales via scheduled Zoom/phone call
Offer price point high enough to warrant a qualification call
claims.mechanism: Repetitive verbal presentations cause both seller disengagement (sounds rehearsed) and buyer disengagement (zones out); a recorded VSL delivers the identical pitch with full visuals every time, freeing the live call for personalized decision-making dialogue.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that founder-led selling outperforms a hired salesperson in early-stage businesses for three compounding reasons: the founder is the most convicted, typically closes at the highest rate, and generates real-time feedback on whether conversion failures stem from pricing, copy, avatar targeting, or the sales process itself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Early-stage business (pre-capacity constraint on sales call volume)
Founder is capable of conducting calls
claims.mechanism: Conviction translates directly into close rate; a founder's product belief is intrinsically higher than a hired rep's; additionally, the founder's direct exposure to objections produces actionable signal for marketing and offer refinement that a rep's filtered report cannot replicate.
bounded_by: Once the founder cannot physically take all calls due to volume, hiring a salesperson and shifting the founder to trainer-multiplier role is warranted.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends testing ad spend at a rate of 2x the allowable CAC (based on 30-day cash collected from one customer) per campaign before shutting an ad off. This absorbs early campaign inefficiency and provides enough signal to identify winning hooks and creative variations before scaling.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: New ad campaign test (not scaled proven winner)
Allowable CAC = 30-day cash collected per customer
claims.mechanism: Early campaigns have inherent inefficiency; cutting spend before the 2x threshold produces a false negative because the winning ad variation may not have been discovered yet; absorbing the inefficiency during testing prevents premature campaign termination.

numbers.axis: ad spend threshold before shutting off a test campaign

anchors.region: Hormozi minimum test budget per campaign
example: customer generates $100 in first 30 days
anchors.value: run ad to $200 before shutting off if getting leads

bounded_by: Apply to test campaigns only; once a winning ad is identified, spend can be scaled aggressively.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi distinguishes between three types of lead magnets: (1) reveal a real problem the prospect didn't know they had, (2) provide a free trial or sample of the solution, (3) give one step of a multi-step process. All three generate trust by demonstrating authority before asking for a sale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Moving prospects from low trust to high trust before presenting a sale increases conversion because authority and perceived competence are demonstrated rather than claimed.
bounded_by: Lead magnets add a step to the funnel and are most valuable when CAC is high relative to offer price; high-brand-equity inbound businesses may not need them.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that businesses should track ad performance all the way through to final sale LTV, not just opt-in volume or front-end sales volume, because the lead magnet that costs more per lead may close at a higher rate and produce superior total revenue per lead.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: A/B testing two lead magnets against each other
claims.mechanism: Front-end opt-in rate and back-end LTV are not correlated predictably; a lead magnet that attracts a profit-motivated avatar may cost 3x more per lead but close 5x more frequently, making it the superior performer only visible at the LTV level.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that the purpose of having a front-end and back-end offer is primarily to pull cash forward (reduce payback period) and offset advertising and labor spend during the sales cycle, not simply to have multiple products. For products where customers have enough information to buy the high-ticket item directly (e.g., fully inbound, brand-warmed audiences), a front-end offer adds unnecessary complexity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cold traffic advertising with significant ad spend
Long sales cycle with labor cost accumulation
claims.mechanism: Every day between ad spend and cash collection is a working-capital drag; a low-ticket front-end offer that closes in one call accelerates cash recovery and funds further customer acquisition without external capital.
bounded_by: Fully inbound, brand-warmed audiences may not need the front-end step and can go directly to the premium offer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that recurring revenue products and services face a structural churn challenge in consulting and education: once the client has learned or implemented the core transformation, they no longer need the service. Businesses should either accept this and price the one-time engagement to generate good margin, or design a genuine consumables-based reason to stay (e.g., ongoing staff training for high-turnover industries).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service delivers a finite transformation (e.g., a cocktail menu redesign)
claims.mechanism: Education and consulting businesses graduate clients; once the implementation is complete, there is no genuine consumable pulling the client back. Forced recurring pricing without genuine recurring value drives early cancellation.
bounded_by: High-turnover industries (e.g., hospitality) create natural re-engagement opportunities through ongoing staff training needs.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that above-the-fold content on a direct response landing page should contain only the headline, sub-headline, image, and opt-in, with no brand logo or company name, because cold-traffic visitors have no existing brand relationship and every element that does not move them toward the opt-in is wasted real estate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Cold visitors have zero brand familiarity; a logo or business name takes up prime visual real estate while providing no conversion value to someone who doesn't know the brand; every non-CTA element dilutes attention toward the opt-in.
bounded_by: Does not apply to landing pages receiving warm or referral traffic where brand recognition adds credibility.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the sub-headline on a direct response landing page should address the single largest concern a prospect has about believing the headline promise, rather than listing features or describing the company.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: After a bold headline claim, the prospect's next thought is their biggest skepticism or obstacle; addressing it preemptively in the sub-headline removes the mental objection before it triggers an exit.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that spreading a discount across multiple payments (e.g., $1,500 off per quarter for four quarters) is superior to applying it as a single deep first-payment discount because the spread discount commits the buyer to a longer relationship and avoids the pattern of easy first-payment yes followed by early cancellation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Seller offering a discount to close
claims.mechanism: A large single-payment discount lowers the price to a level that attracts price-sensitive buyers who are likely to cancel after one period; spreading the discount retains the commitment signal at each payment while still providing total discount value.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that if the offer, avatar call-out, lead magnet, and landing page are all corrected simultaneously, it is realistic to increase a cold-traffic landing page conversion rate from ~7% to ~30% and a sales close rate from 6% to 30–50%, which in combination represent a potential tripling of total revenue from the same ad spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to Unfiltered Hospitality's specific situation (cold traffic, B2B service, restaurant/bar sector)
Founder taking all sales calls personally

numbers.axis: revenue impact of simultaneous funnel + offer + avatar fixes

bounded_by: Results depend on execution quality, market conditions, and founder effort; no guarantee.

examples.text: Ben (Unfiltered Hospitality) ran an ad that sent cold traffic directly to a $30,000 consulting offer with no lead magnet and no funnel warming. His landing page converted at ~7% opt-in and his sales close rate was 6%. His CAC reached ~$12,000 on a $30,000 offer, producing an LTV-to-CAC ratio of only 1.7x. Alex Hormozi used this case to illustrate the offer-funnel mismatch: cold prospects cannot justify a $30,000 commitment in one or two calls with no prior trust established.

Alex Hormozi described testing a lead magnet at $97 versus $47 and finding that the $97 version converted at nearly the same opt-in volume as $47 but collected twice the revenue. More importantly, buyers of the $97 version were substantially more likely to purchase back-end higher-ticket offers. Hormozi noted he had no theoretical explanation for why paid lead magnets increased LTV; he cited it as a reason to test all the way through LTV rather than optimizing on front-end conversion rate alone.

Alex Hormozi walked Ben through his own landing page live and demonstrated the double opt-in friction problem: after submitting a name and email on the first page, the funnel asked Ben to re-enter the same information on the second page. Hormozi framed this as a classic case of a business owner who had not personally gone through their own sales process since building it. He noted that this type of bad friction (non-qualifying) drives away both good and bad prospects without any filtering benefit.

Ben's program performance retainer (recurring quarterly service post-cocktail-consulting) was churning after approximately two payments. Alex Hormozi diagnosed the cause as the team not consistently completing the scorecard and KPI calls that were supposed to demonstrate value to clients. Hormozi suggested that if Ben's team logged into clients' POS systems directly and presented their own data back to them each month, clients would perceive a far higher level of expertise and accountability, dramatically reducing churn.

Alex Hormozi proposed a specific pricing-audit front-end offer for Unfiltered Hospitality at $5,800. The product would audit the bar's current pricing against market comparables, adjust prices within the PMS, and back-calculate how much additional profit the client would have made the prior year with those prices. This front-end product was chosen because it delivers a fast (15–30 day), easy, immediately measurable financial result that creates a natural seeding moment for the $30,000 core offer: 'If you liked what we did with pricing, wait until you see what we can do for the entire program.'

practices.text: Replace YouTube-hosted videos in your funnel with Vimeo or another third-party host to keep viewers on your page and maintain a professional appearance.
Regularly go through your own opt-in and sales funnel end-to-end as if you were a cold prospect to identify friction points, broken steps, and double data-entry that erode conversion.
Have your director of operations instruct prospects to watch the VSL before the sales call, and begin the call by asking if they watched it; if they have not, pause the call until they do.
On the post-booking confirmation page, include a second VSL focused on common concerns and objections (call prep content) rather than showing the same pre-booking VSL again.
Structure ad copy using specific avatar call-outs (e.g., '$4 million-plus per year restaurant owners') as the first line before any pain hook or benefit statement.

Frame copy around the moments a prospect experiences the pain or the relief, rather than listing features or process steps, to minimize the mental effort required to translate your promise into their reality.
Split-test two distinct lead magnets (e.g., cocktail-focused vs. profit-calculator-focused) in an ABA format and measure performance all the way through to final sale LTV before declaring a winner.

When upselling after delivering a quick-win front-end product, make the first upsell attempt at the moment the client sees their first measurable result, the second attempt approximately one week later, and the third as a final last-chance offer before the engagement window closes.

Operate with the principle of never asking the client for money you have not already made them: deliver measurable value from the front-end engagement before presenting the price of the back-end upsell.

For consulting businesses with high-turnover client staff, consider securing a login to the client's POS or management system to pull data and present it back to the client monthly, demonstrating ongoing value without relying on the client to self-report.
